lesson.title: Eight Groups of Four: Reading and Compressing an IPv6 Address
lesson.summary: An IPv6 address is written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons, with two compression shortcuts, leading-zero suppression and a single double colon for consecutive zero groups, that make the 128-bit address readable.
lesson.body:
IPv6, as introduced already, uses 128-bit addresses, four times longer than IPv4's 32 bits, so writing one out in dotted-decimal form the way IPv4 does would be unwieldy. Instead, IPv6 addresses are written in hexadecimal, split into eight groups of four hex digits each, since 4 bits per hex digit times 4 digits times 8 groups equals 128 bits, with each group separated from its neighbors by a colon. A full, uncompressed IPv6 address looks like this: 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329. Each of those eight groups, 2001, 0db8, 0000, 0000, 0000, ff00, 0042, and 8329, represents 16 bits, and hexadecimal digits can be any of 0 through 9 or a through f, case-insensitive, though lowercase is the conventional style.

Writing out every leading zero in every group makes addresses long and hard to scan visually, so IPv6 defines two compression rules that any conforming implementation must support. The first is leading-zero suppression within a single group: 0db8 can be written as db8, and 0042 can be written as 42, dropping leading zeros but never dropping a group entirely this way, so a group of all zeros, 0000, compresses to a single 0 under this rule alone. The second, more powerful rule is double-colon compression: one or more consecutive groups that are entirely zero can be replaced with a double colon, but this shorthand can be used only once per address. Applying both rules to the example above, 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329 first becomes 2001:db8:0:0:0:ff00:42:8329 after leading-zero suppression, and then the three consecutive all-zero groups collapse to a double colon, giving the fully compressed form 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329.

The rule limiting the double colon to a single use per address is not arbitrary; it exists so that any compressed address can be unambiguously expanded back to its full 128-bit form. If two separate runs of zero groups could each be replaced by their own double colon, a parser reading the compressed address would have no way to know how many zero groups belonged in each gap, since the total must always add up to exactly eight groups. With only one double colon permitted, the parser simply counts the groups present on both sides of it and inserts exactly enough zero groups in the middle to reach eight total. For example, the loopback address, written in full as 0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001, compresses unambiguously to double-colon-1, since there is only one non-zero group and it sits at the very end.

IPv6 addresses are also commonly written with a CIDR-style prefix length, exactly like the notation covered earlier for IPv4, to indicate how many leading bits identify the network versus the interface: 2001:db8::/32 identifies a 32-bit network prefix commonly delegated to an organization, while an individual interface address within that network is typically given a /64, reflecting IPv6's convention of using the first 64 bits for the network portion and the last 64 bits for the interface identifier. That fixed 64 and 64 split, and how the interface portion of the address gets filled in, matters directly for both the address types and the autoconfiguration mechanisms covered in the next two sections.
